subject: TTFT & streaming requirements — post-call recap and next steps
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Sandeep Rao <sandeep@fintech.ai>, Jill Harper <jill.harper@acme.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>, Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.com>

Subject: TTFT & streaming requirements — post-call recap and next steps

Hi Sandeep / Jill —

Thanks for taking the time today. Quick recap from our call and proposed next steps so we’re all aligned on TTFT/streaming SLOs and what we need to validate on our side: 

Key targets you called out:
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT): p95 ≤ 120 ms for single-stream interactive requests (avg request size ~60 tokens).
- Streaming behavior: client needs a streaming-first UX (incremental tokens as they’re produced). Preferred transport: WebSocket; SSE is acceptable for MVP.
- Chunk cadence: target visible update cadence ~150–300 ms (small token batches, low buffering).
- Concurrency/throughput: peak concurrent streams ~200, sustained ~80–100; target 250 requests/sec peak throughput for batched non-streaming calls.
- Model footprint: planning to run a 7B open model variant with int8 quantization; customer will consider larger models later.

Open questions for Sandeep that will help our engineering bench: 
1) Are there hard network traversal constraints (mTLS, proxying, client IP ranges) we should test against?
2) For streaming sessions, what’s the expected request/response size distribution (tokens in / tokens out)?
3) Do you require guaranteed ordering/at-least-once semantics over WebSocket?

Attachments: TTFT_benchmark.pdf (Redwood sample benchmarks), customer_stream_trace.pcap (you mentioned a capture)

Next steps I propose: 
- Aditya + Dev will run a lab benchmark with a 7B quantized config to validate p95 TTFT at our infra (target ETA: 48–72 hrs).
- We’ll validate chunk cadence over WebSocket vs SSE and share a short recording of frame timings.
- Follow-up call: propose Tue 2027-06-08 10:00 PT to review numbers and any security questions (SOC2 evidence / network requirements).

If that all looks right, we’ll schedule the lab run and I’ll share the test harness and minimal sample client for you to run locally.

Thanks —
Marissa Cole

Marissa —

Thanks for the recap and clear next steps. A few quick answers while we prep internally: 
- Peak concurrency of 200 is accurate for our busiest window; sustained usually ~80.
- Average request size: 40–80 input tokens. Average response: ~180 tokens. We’re sensitive to the first visible token arriving quickly for UX.
- Preference: WebSocket for our long-lived sessions (we use it today for real-time updates). SSE would be fine for short-lived requests but doesn’t fit well with our existing client infra.
- Security: we need mutual TLS (mTLS) for private endpoints; also SOC2 evidence + contract redlines are in motion with our legal team.

Attached: sample_stream_trace.pcap — contains 10 sessions from production that illustrate chunking behavior.

Looking forward to the bench numbers. Tue 06/08 10:00 PT works for us.

Subject: Re: Fwd: TTFT & streaming requirements — post-call recap and next steps

Marissa —

Quick bench notes from the lab run (summary, full logs attached to deal record):

Summary config used:
- Model: open-7b-v2 int8 quantized
- Execution: single-stream streaming path (no batching), WebSocket transport
- HW: 1x A100 40GB equivalent per 8 streams; autoscaling simulated
- Network: mTLS enabled (openssl cipher default)

Results (representative):
- p50 TTFT: 62 ms
- p95 TTFT: 118 ms (meets target of ≤120 ms)
- Chunk cadence observed: median ~160 ms, 90th ~240 ms
- Impact of batching: enabling continuous batching on the same endpoint increased p95 TTFT to ~310 ms — recommend disabling batching for streaming endpoints and using dedicated streaming workers.
- mTLS overhead: ~6–12 ms added to cold-session TTFT during TLS handshake; warm sessions within threshold.

Recommendations / next steps:
1) Expose a streaming-only endpoint (WebSocket) that bypasses batching and pins a lightweight worker pool.
2) Use a chunk-buffer policy that flushes every 120–180 ms for best tradeoff (can tune to 150 ms for smoother UX).
3) For peak concurrency 200, propose 25 x 8-stream workers (estimate; will refine with more load testing).
4) Share full timing traces and a small Node/Go sample client for Sandeep to reproduce locally.

I’ll attach raw timing CSVs to the deal link and schedule the bench demo for Tue’s call.
